cover.headline: A diversified compounder trading below its own history; the catch is asset quality in vehicles and a regulator now looking at insurance commissions
cover.lead: Cholamandalam (Chola), the Murugappa group's lender, has grown profit ~25% a year for a decade at a 19-21% return on equity, moving from a vehicle financier to an eight-engine lender: vehicles (53% of AUM), loans against property and home loans (33%), and newer small-business, consumer and gold loans. Q1FY27 was strong (profit +46%, ROE 21.2%, credit cost down to 1.5%), but Stage 3 loans rose to 3.29% and vehicle-finance Stage 3 to 4.05%. The street values Chola on **P/B (3.8-4.0x FY28E book)**. We forecast EPS of ₹80.6 / ₹94.6 / ₹113.4 for FY27-29E at ~19-20% ROE, including a haircut for IRDAI's proposed caps on insurance commission. Applying **3.2x to Sep-28E book of ₹587** (its own 3.4x median since 2021, adjusted for the sector's −4.5% move) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY**, only just above our 15% line. The intrinsic cross-checks (justified P/B ₹1,288, residual income ₹1,454) are below the price, which already implies a ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}} ROE for ever. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: Eight engines, all firing for the first time
arguments.p: In FY25 growth came from three businesses; by Q1FY27 all eight were growing: vehicles +19%, LAP +23%, home loans +22%, SME +39%, SBPL +40%, CSEL +12% and gold to ₹2,143 cr from ₹97 cr. Guidance is 20-23% AUM growth ("23% ... doable"); we model {{F.aumGrowth.0|pct}} / {{F.aumGrowth.1|pct}} / {{F.aumGrowth.2|pct}}. Equity grows ~20% a year from retained profit, so growth needs no new capital at this pace.

arguments.h: Credit costs are turning, but the evidence is mixed
arguments.p: Loan losses were 1.6% of assets in FY26 before a ₹200 cr overlay (1.7% with it) and 1.5% in Q1FY27, meeting FY27 guidance in the seasonally weakest quarter. Against that, Stage 2+3 rose 49bp in the quarter and vehicle-finance Stage 3 hit 4.05%. We model {{F.creditCost.0|pct}} of AUM (about 1.4-1.5% on the company's asset basis), keep the overlay, and do not extrapolate Q1.

arguments.h: Two new risks the street had not priced on 30 September
arguments.p: IRDAI's 23-Sep-2026 consultation proposes capping commission on loan-linked insurance at ~2-5%. Chola earned ₹1,136 cr of insurance commission in FY26, 16.3% of pre-tax profit; we cut fee income by ~0.15% of AUM from FY28E. Rate hikes are the second: Chola is wholesale-funded and AA+ rated (not AAA), and most economists expected a repo hike in October.

arguments.h: Valuation: below its history, not cheap on fundamentals
arguments.p: At ₹1,620 the stock trades at 3.0x our FY28E book and 17.1x FY28E EPS, against a 3.4x median forward P/B since 2021, after a ~12% fall in the September sell-off. Our 3.2x Sep-28E book gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}). The margin over the BUY line is thin: at 3.1x the target would be a HOLD.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): management promised the usual Q2-Q3 fall in Stage 2 and 3 after Q1's seasonal rise; disbursements should normalise after the cheque-clearance change.
IRDAI's insurance-distribution reforms: consultation paper of 23-Sep-2026, comments due 25-Oct-2026; caps of ~2-5% on loan-linked commission would hit Chola's fee income.
RBI's October 2026 policy: most economists polled expected a 25bp repo hike; the CFO already assumes 25-50bp and a 5-10bp rise in funding costs in H2FY27.
Gold loans: 360 new branches and an AUM target of ~₹5,000 cr by Mar-27 (₹2,143 cr in Jun-2026).
The ₹200 cr management overlay: kept intact in Q1; management will "take a view on it at the end of this financial year".

sections.title: A small-town lender with eight businesses, built on a vehicle-finance network

blocks.p: Cholamandalam Investment and Finance (Chola) is the lending arm of the Murugappa group, a Chennai conglomerate whose listed companies include Coromandel International, Tube Investments and Carborundum Universal. It is an upper-layer NBFC (the RBI's tier for the largest non-bank lenders) and does not take public deposits. It makes money the way every lender does: it borrows at ~7.4% (our measure, FY26), lends at ~14% on average, earns another ~1.3% of loans in fees (mostly insurance commission and loan fees), and keeps what is left after operating costs (~3.2% of loans) and loan losses (~1.5-1.7%). In FY26 interest income was ₹28,403 cr of its ₹31,073 cr revenue.

Its customers are small road-transport operators, farmers, self-employed traders and small manufacturers in small towns: 87% of its 1,820 branches are in tier 3-6 towns, and it served 5.2 million customers in Jun-2026. Vehicle finance is the original business and the network everything else runs on: the LAP, home-loan, CSEL, SBPL and SME teams sit inside vehicle-finance branches. Only gold loans have stand-alone branches. Group holding company Cholamandalam Financial Holdings owns 43.7%; the promoter group 49.2%.

blocks.callout: **Why this matters:** Chola is one network selling seven products, which keeps costs down (new businesses borrow vehicle-finance branches) and lets growth shift between products. In FY24-FY25, when vehicle demand slowed, LAP, home loans and SBPL carried growth; in FY26-27 vehicles came back. The flip side: the new products are riskier (CSEL lost 6.3% of its loans in FY26) or not yet seasoned (SME, SBPL, gold), and all of them lean on the same small-town borrower whose cash flows move with the farm and freight cycle.

sections.title: Five decades in vehicles, five years of diversification, and two capital raises

blocks.p: Chola started in 1978 as an equipment lessor, was in a joint venture with Singapore's DBS Bank in 2006-2011, and spent most of its history as a vehicle financier with LAP on the side. Home loans started in 2013. The decisive step was FY22-23, when it launched three new businesses at once (CSEL, SBPL, SME) and grew AUM 38% in FY23 and 37% in FY24. The record shows a pattern: equity is raised every few years to fund a growth spurt (FY20, FY24), and credit costs rise when the vehicle cycle turns (FY20-21, FY25-26) but have never wiped out profit.

sections.title: Vehicle sales hit records in Q1, but rates are rising and the regulators are busy

blocks.p: Half of Chola's book rides on India's vehicle cycle, and in Q1FY27 that cycle was strong. Per SIAM and ICRA data in Chola's presentation, heavy trucks grew 13% (their best Q1 ever), light trucks 18%, small commercial vehicles 31%, cars and utility vehicles 26% (best Q1, helped by the cut in GST rates), two-wheelers 20%, tractors 19% (record quarterly sales on good farm cash flows) and construction equipment 9%. The used-vehicle market, where Chola earns its highest yields, keeps formalising. The FY24-FY25 slowdown that management called a "down cycle" for vehicles is over, at least for now; the risk is a weak monsoon (the forecast was 92% of normal) hitting tractor and rural transport borrowers in H2.

The money side has turned less friendly. September 2026 was a bad month for Indian markets: the Nifty fell ~5% by 28-Sep on foreign selling, Brent was ~$106, US 10-year yields 5.2%, and most economists polled expected the RBI to raise the repo rate by 25bp to 5.5% in October, the first hike since Feb-2023. Listed NBFCs fell 4-16% between 31-Jul and 30-Sep-2026; Chola fell ~12% in the second half of September. Wholesale-funded lenders like Chola feel rate hikes first, through bank loans priced off MCLR and new bond issues.

Among the listed lenders we track, Chola is the third-largest by market value (₹1.39 lakh cr on 30-Sep-2026, behind Bajaj Finance and Shriram Finance). Its FY26 ROE (19.3%) was second only to Muthoot Finance's, but its return on assets (2.3%) was well below Bajaj Finance, Shriram, SBI Cards and Muthoot (3.3-6.5%): Chola earns its ROE with leverage (assets 8x equity) rather than high margins, because its loans are secured and its borrowers are priced competitively by banks.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** demand is not Chola's problem; vehicles are at record highs and the small-business and affordable-housing markets in tier 3-6 towns are underpenetrated. The constraints are the **cost of money** (rising, and Chola has no deposit franchise), **asset quality at the bottom of the pyramid** (small transport operators and micro-merchants feel a weak monsoon or a diesel shock first) and **regulation of fee income**, which has been a quiet profit driver.

sections.title: Tailwind test: which trends actually help Chola's returns?

blocks.p: An industry trend only matters to a shareholder if the company turns it into profit. We score each one.

Yes

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the tailwinds that matter most for FY27 (the vehicle up-cycle and lower credit costs) are cyclical; the structural ones (mortgages for small businesses, cross-sell across a 5 million customer base) are real but slow. Two headwinds arrived in September: higher rates and the IRDAI proposal. That is why we model ROE flat at ~19-20% (FY27E {{F.roe.0|pct}}), not rising, even with the credit cycle in Chola's favour.

sections.title: Growth now comes from eight engines, and the mix is tilting away from vehicles

blocks.p: Chola disbursed ₹1,11,642 cr of loans in FY26 (+11%) and ₹29,612 cr in Q1FY27 (+22%), to 5.2 million customers through 1,820 branches. Business AUM grew 21% in FY26 to ₹2,24,334 cr and 22% in the year to Jun-2026. The shape of growth has changed: in FY25 three engines (LAP, home loans, SBPL) carried the company while vehicles slowed; in FY26 vehicles came back, and by Q1FY27 every business was growing. New businesses (CSEL, SME, SBPL, gold) are 13.6% of AUM, up from 2% in FY22.

sections.title: Vehicle finance: back in growth, still the biggest source of losses

blocks.p: Vehicle finance is the core: ₹1,24,132 cr of AUM in Jun-2026 (+19%), ₹62,123 cr of disbursements in FY26 (+15%) and ₹16,503 cr in Q1FY27 (+21%). Chola sits in the middle of the market: new and used light and small commercial vehicles for small road-transport operators, cars and utility vehicles for taxi and self-employed buyers, tractors, two- and three-wheelers and construction equipment. Heavy trucks, where large fleet owners and banks dominate, are only 5-7% of the book. Used vehicles carry the highest yields.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** vehicles are the swing factor. The segment earned a 2.9% pre-tax ROA in FY26, below the company's 3.3%, because loan losses (1.9-2.2%) are the highest of any large business. Management says the three-year "down cycle" ended in Q4FY26, and Q1 PBT rose 50%. But Stage 3 rose from 3.52% to 4.05% over five quarters, and Nomura notes Jun-2026 was the worst first quarter since Covid. We model vehicles growing ~18% and do not assume their losses fall much: a weak monsoon or a diesel spike would land here first.

sections.title: Loans against property and home loans: the quiet profit engine

blocks.p: Loans against property (LAP, ₹54,130 cr, +23%) and affordable home loans (₹23,644 cr, +22%) are a third of the book and, by our arithmetic on the segment P&Ls, 42% of FY26 segment profit (39% of company PBT). LAP lends to small businesses against their home or shop; home loans go to self-employed and salaried buyers in small towns. Both are secured on property, so losses are low (LAP 0.3% of assets in FY26, home loans 1.0%), and both earn more on assets than vehicles (pre-tax ROA 3.9% and 4.2%). The CFO said LAP alone is ~30% of company PBT and should stay there.

blocks.p: Two things to watch. First, **disbursement growth is weak**: home-loan disbursements have sat at ₹1,800-2,000 cr a quarter for two years and grew 2% in Q1FY27 (LAP +2%), partly because Chola now books a loan only when the cheque clears (like-for-like ~20%, CFO). AUM still grows 22-23% because loans run off slowly, but that gap cannot last for ever; guidance is 12-15% disbursement growth in home loans. Second, **LAP Stage 3 rose** from 2.24% to 2.58% in the quarter, the largest sequential rise of any segment (Nomura). Management says LAP losses will stay ~0.3% a year because property collateral can be enforced under SARFAESI (for loans above ₹20 lakh).

blocks.callout: **Our view:** mortgages are Chola's best business and the reason we expect ROE to hold even as vehicle growth slows. We model LAP and home loans growing 23-25% a year (guidance 25-30%), with almost no margin pressure. The risk is competition: banks and housing-finance companies price LAP and home loans aggressively, and Chola's edge is distribution in towns banks do not serve, not cheaper money.

sections.title: The new businesses: high yields, one costly lesson (fintech loans), and gold as the next bet

blocks.p: In FY22-23 Chola launched three businesses at once: **CSEL** (consumer and small-enterprise loans: unsecured personal, business and professional loans plus consumer-durable finance), **SBPL** (small secured loans to micro-merchants) and **SME** (loans to small manufacturers and traders). Gold loans followed in FY26. Together they were ₹31,680 cr in Jun-2026, 13.6% of AUM. They were meant to lift returns above the company average; so far that has worked in SBPL, is starting to work in CSEL, and is not yet visible in SME or gold.

pair.title: New businesses: ₹1,600 cr to ₹31,700 cr in four years
CSEL: loan losses falling after the fintech exit

blocks.p: CSEL grew fast in FY23-FY24 partly through fintech partnerships, and those loans went bad: CSEL lost 6.3% of its assets in FY26 and earned a pre-tax ROA of only 1.6%. Chola shut the partnership channel (the fintech book was 1.5% of Chola's loans in May-2025 and ₹300-400 cr was left to run off in May-2026), tightened its scorecards and now covers ~80% of its ~₹5,000 cr business-loan book with CGTMSE, the government credit guarantee (₹38 cr of guarantee fees in Q4FY26). The result: CSEL AUM grew only 4% in FY26, but losses fell to 4.7% and ROA rose to 3.3% in Q1FY27. Management expects ROA above 3% this year and ~20% asset growth by Q4FY27.

blocks.h: SBPL and SME: high returns, unproven through a cycle

blocks.p: SBPL lends under ₹20 lakh to micro-merchants against property, at ~25% yields; it earns a 7-8% pre-tax ROA even with 2-3% loan losses. Its weakness is collections: loans this small cannot be enforced under SARFAESI, so Chola sells bad loans to asset-reconstruction companies, and Stage 3 swings with those sales (4.70% in Jun-2026, from 3.53% in March). SME is the opposite: low yields (13%) and a thin 2.1-2.3% ROA, with Stage 3 rising from 3.22% to 3.83% in the quarter. Both businesses are less than four years old; neither has been through a downturn.

blocks.h: Gold loans: a fast start, a long payback

blocks.p: Gold loans reached ₹2,143 cr in Jun-2026 from 171 stand-alone branches (119 in March). Chola plans 360 more in FY27 and targets ~₹5,000 cr of AUM by Mar-27 (we build ₹5,000 cr, then ₹11,200 cr in FY29E). The average loan is ~₹2 lakh, 90% of customers are new to Chola, branches hold ₹12-15 cr each, and management expects this year's branches to break even by the end of next year. It is a sensible use of the brand in a market dominated by Muthoot and Manappuram and by banks, but at <1% of AUM it will not move group profit until FY28-29, and the branch build adds to costs now.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the new businesses are doing what they were designed to do, raising the blended yield, but the CSEL episode shows the cost of growing unsecured loans through partners. We model them growing faster than the group (15-30% a year, gold faster) and treat their credit cost as structurally higher, which is why our group credit cost edges up to {{F.creditCost.2|pct}} in FY29E even as vehicles stabilise.

sections.title: NIM is back above 8% of assets on cheaper funding; rate hikes now push the other way

blocks.p: Chola reports its margin on average total assets: 7.5% in FY24, 7.7% in FY25, 8.0% in FY26 and 8.2% in Q1FY27. On our basis (NII ÷ average business AUM) NIM was {{fin.nim.9|pct}}, {{fin.nim.10|pct}} and {{fin.nim.11|pct}} in FY24-26. The improvement came from funding: the RBI cut rates through 2025 and Chola's cost of funds fell from {{fin.costOfFunds.10|pct}} in FY25 to {{fin.costOfFunds.11|pct}} in FY26 (our measure), while the yield on AUM fell less ({{fin.yieldOnAum.10|pct}} to {{fin.yieldOnAum.11|pct}}) because most vehicle loans are fixed-rate. That cushion has run its course: the CFO expects funding costs flat for FY27 overall but 5-10bp higher in H2, assuming a 25-50bp repo hike.

sections.title: Asset quality: credit cost is improving, but bad loans are still edging up

blocks.p: Loan losses rose from 1.0% of assets in FY24 to 1.4% in FY25 and 1.7% in FY26 (1.6% before the ₹200 cr overlay), well above the 1.3% management guided for FY26. Two things drove it: a vehicle "down cycle" in FY24-FY25 and the fintech-sourced CSEL loans. Q1FY27 brought the credit cost down to 1.5%, meeting the full-year guidance in the seasonally weakest quarter, and Stage 2 (loans 30-90 days overdue) is 33bp lower than a year ago. But Stage 3 is not falling: 3.29% in Jun-2026 vs 3.16% a year earlier, and 4.50% on the RBI's stricter NPA definition.

sections.title: Funding: diversified and liquid, but AA+, wholesale and more expensive than a bank

blocks.p: Chola borrowed ₹2,20,247 cr in Jun-2026 (standalone). About half comes from banks (much of it priority-sector lending, where Chola has bargaining power), the rest from bonds and debentures (private and public), commercial paper, securitisation, foreign borrowings and subordinated Tier II debt. It takes no public deposits. It is rated AA+ by ICRA (outlook positive), CARE and India Ratings, one notch below the AAA of Bajaj Finance and bank-owned NBFCs; the CFO said peers got AAA "by leveraging explicit parental support", which the Murugappa group does not provide for Chola's funding. On our measure Chola paid {{fin.costOfFunds.11|pct}} on its borrowings in FY26, against ~7.3% for Bajaj Finance.

sections.title: Capital: self-funding at ~20% growth, with the CCDs now fully converted

blocks.p: Capital adequacy was 19.81% in Jun-2026 (Tier 1 14.81%) against RBI minimums of 15% and 10%. Management's rule is explicit: it will consider raising equity "if our Tier 1 ratio were to approach 13%", and it expects to fund growth internally as long as pre-tax ROTA is ~3.5% and growth stays below 23-25%. Chola retains ~97% of profit (dividend ₹2 a share since FY21), so equity grows ~20% a year from profit alone, roughly matching AUM growth. Our model keeps business AUM at {{fin.leverage.12|n2}}-{{fin.leverage.14|n2}}x equity in FY27-29E, close to {{fin.leverage.11|n2}}x in FY26.

The last capital raise was the Oct-2023 composite QIP: ₹2,000 cr of shares and ₹2,000 cr of 7.5% compulsorily convertible debentures (CCDs). The CCDs converted at 15-16.5% discounts to the market price: ₹1,370 cr in FY26 (at ₹1,369-1,393), ₹200 cr in Jul-2026 (₹1,476) and the last ₹430 cr on 30-Sep-2026 (₹1,407.59). The share count rose from 85.2 cr in March to 85.75 cr on 30-Sep-2026; we include the ₹630 cr conversion in FY27E equity. Converting at a discount to a price of ~4.6x book still added to book value per share.

The trade-off is the dividend: at ~3% of profit it is among the lowest of any large Indian financial. Shareholders are paid in book growth, which only works while ROE stays well above the cost of equity. If growth ran at the 24% of our bull case for long, Tier 1 would drift toward 13% and Chola would raise equity, as it did in FY20 and FY24.

Chola earns less per rupee of loans than Bajaj Finance (yields ~14% vs ~15.5%, and a higher funding cost) but runs ~7.5x leverage on secured loans, against ~4.5x for Bajaj, so both end up near 20%. sections.title: Ten years of ~25% profit growth with only one down year

blocks.p: Chola grew net profit from ₹575 cr in FY16 to ₹5,233 cr in FY26, about 25% a year, and book value per share from ₹47 to ₹357, about 22% a year. The only down year was FY20 (−12%), when Covid provisions pushed loan losses to 1.6% of assets; profit then grew 44% in FY21 and 42% in FY22. Since FY23 the pattern has been steady: profit +24%, +28%, +25% and +23% a year, as fast loan growth (21-38% a year) was partly eaten by rising credit costs in vehicle finance and the new unsecured loans. Return on equity has stayed in a narrow 19-21% band for five years.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** Chola is a steady compounder, not a cyclical. Profit growth has been 23-28% for four years running, and we forecast {{F.patGrowth.0|pct}} in FY27E (Q1 was +46% off a weak base) and ~18-20% a year after that. What has not improved is the cost of running the business: cost-to-income went from 32% in FY21 to ~40% as Chola built six new businesses and, from FY26, a gold-loan branch network. Operating leverage is the missing lever; management does not expect it for "another year or so".

sections.title: Competitive advantage: a narrow moat in small-town distribution and collections, none in funding

blocks.p: A lender's moat shows up as a lasting gap between what it earns on loans and what it pays for money, costs and losses. Chola has earned a 2.2-2.9% ROA on assets and a 17-21% ROE in every year since FY19 except the Covid year, with leverage doing much of the work. We test where its edge comes from.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Chola has a narrow but real moat: it reaches and collects from small-town borrowers that banks cannot serve profitably, and it has repeated that model across vehicles, property and now gold. It does not have a cost-of-funds advantage, its unsecured experiment showed limits, and its ROE depends on running ~7-8x leverage on secured loans. blocks.p: Q1FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026) was Chola's best quarter on returns in two years: disbursements +22% to ₹29,612 cr, business AUM +22%, net income margin 8.2% of assets (+42bp), loan losses 1.5% (from 1.8%), pre-tax ROTA 3.7% and ROE 21.2%; profit rose 46% to ₹1,654 cr (standalone). The weak spots: Stage 3 up 24bp in the quarter to 3.29% (seasonal, says management; "worse than vehicle-finance peers", says Emkay), opex up 23% with gold-branch openings, and disbursements in mortgages flattered down by a one-time change in when loans are counted.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean audits, but insurance commission, related parties and recoveries need watching

blocks.p: We rate accounting **AMBER**. Joint auditors KKC & Associates and B.K. Khare & Co gave an unmodified opinion on FY26 (key audit matters: expected credit loss and IT controls), and disclosure is good (segment P&Ls, stage-wise provisions by product). Five things deserve attention:

bullets: **Insurance commission and related parties.** Insurance agency commission was ₹1,136 cr in FY26, 16.3% of PBT. Borrower accident and hospital covers are placed with group insurer Chola MS General Insurance. In Dec-2025 the portal Cobrapost alleged ₹10,262 cr of related-party routing and ₹25,000 cr of cash deposits; Chola called this "malicious and baseless" (cash comes from small transport operators' EMIs) and said all related-party transactions are disclosed. We found no regulatory action by 30-Sep-2026, but IRDAI's proposed commission caps now put this income line in play.

**Recoveries sit outside credit cost.** Recoveries of loans written off earlier (₹415 cr in FY26, ₹254 cr in FY25) are booked as other income, not netted against loan losses. Net of them, FY26 credit cost would be ~0.2pp lower; reported credit cost is therefore conservative, but profit leans on recoveries more than the credit-cost line suggests.

**Provisioning discretion.** The ₹200 cr overlay (Q4FY26) and the once-a-year reset of default and loss-given-default assumptions (moved from the March to the December quarter) give management room to smooth profit. Releasing the overlay would add ~2% to FY27 profit.

**Lumpy gains and a recognition change.** Gains on assigning loans were ₹439 cr in FY26 (₹159 cr in FY25), 6% of PBT. From Q1FY27 disbursements are counted only when the cheque clears, which cut reported disbursements and lifts yields slightly. ARC sales in SBPL move Stage 3 between quarters, and ARC receipts in home loans are booked as income while the matching losses run through credit cost.
**Two NPA numbers.** Ind AS Stage 3 (3.29%) and the RBI's stricter NPA (4.50%) differ by ~1.2pp; investors comparing Chola with peers should use the same measure.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a BUY on the street's yardstick, by a thin margin

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** a well-run, diversified small-town lender: eight businesses on one branch network, ROE of 19-21% in every normal year, profit growth of 23-28% for four years, mortgages (a third of the book) earning 4%+ pre-tax ROA, no need for new equity at ~20% growth, and a credit cycle that improved in Q1FY27 (loan losses 1.5% of assets, guidance met in the weakest quarter).

**What you are paying:** 3.0x our FY28E book and 17.1x FY28E EPS, below the stock's 3.4x median forward P/B since 2021 after a ~12% fall in late September. On the street's method that gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}) and a BUY. It is not cheap on fundamentals: at a 13.4% cost of equity the price already implies a ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}} ROE for ever, and our justified P/B (₹1,288) and residual income (₹1,454) are both below the price. You are paying for growth to stay above 20% with ROE near 20%.

What it means
rows: Non-banking financial company: an RBI-regulated lender that cannot take current or savings deposits. The "upper layer" is the RBI's tier for the largest NBFCs, with bank-like rules.

Consumer & small-enterprise loans (unsecured personal, business, professional and consumer-durable loans); secured business & personal loans (small loans against property); loans to small and medium enterprises.
Net interest income = interest earned − interest paid. Net interest margin = NII ÷ average AUM (our basis) or ÷ average assets (Chola's basis).
NII plus fees and other operating income; operating expenses ÷ net total income.
Loan-loss provisions ÷ average AUM (our basis) or average assets (company basis).

assumptions._note: Cholamandalam Investment and Finance (consolidated; subsidiaries are small) lender model, as of 30-Sep-2026 on a Q1FY27 basis. AUM = 'Business AUM' (loans incl. ~1.5% assigned off book; excludes the cash and investments that the company's 'Total AUM' of ₹2.43 lakh cr adds). Sources: Q1FY27 presentation (28-Jul-2026) and call; Q4FY26 presentation (30-Apr-2026) and call (4-May-2026); Annual Reports FY22, FY24, FY26 for revenue splits and impairment; Screener.in for statements. CCD conversion (₹630 cr, Jul and 30-Sep-2026) is in FY27E.

history._why: aum = Business AUM at March (FY18-FY23 from the Q4FY24 presentation's 15-year snapshot, which still used business AUM; FY24-FY26 from the Q1FY27 presentation p13). provisions = impairment of financial instruments in the consolidated P&L (FY21-FY26, annual reports) and loan losses & provisions in the company snapshot for FY18-FY20 (standalone). feeIncome = consolidated revenue from operations less interest income (fees & commission incl. insurance agency commission, net gain on derecognition/assignment, fair-value gains, servicing fees). Screener revenue is ₹3-47 cr higher each year because it also counts interest on tax refunds (FY26 ₹44 cr), so implied interest income is that much above the annual report.

src.FY21-FY22: Annual Report FY22, consolidated P&L (₹ lakh)

base._why: Paid-up capital ₹170.48 cr at 31-Mar-2026 at ₹2 face value (Annual Report FY26, directors' report) = 85.24 cr shares; Screener's FY26 profit ÷ EPS gives 85.21 cr.

assumptions._aumGrowthWhy: FY27 guidance 20-23% (4-May-2026), reaffirmed on 28-Jul with '23% ... doable'; Q1FY27 +22% YoY. Segment guidance: vehicle finance ~18%, LAP and home loans 25-30%, SME and SBPL 30%+, gold AUM ₹2,143 cr to ~₹5,000 cr. We take 22% (upper half; FY26 delivered 21% against 20-25% guidance) and fade 1pp a year as vehicle finance (53% of AUM) grows high-teens.

aumBuild._why: Illustrative segment build (GAM); checked in CHOLAFIN.ctx.js to sum to the model AUM within 1%. Guidance: VF ~18%, LAP/HL 25-30%, SME/SBPL 30%+, gold ~₹5,000 cr by Mar-27. Growth fades 1pp a year; gold in ₹ cr.

assumptions._yieldOnAumWhy: Interest income ÷ average business AUM: 14.0% FY24, 14.4% FY25, 13.9% FY26 (the 2025 repo cuts passed through and more cash earned treasury rates). Q1FY27 revenue ÷ AUM (annualised) was 15.5%, the same as Q1FY26, before the usual drift through the year. Mix moves toward higher-yield CSEL (20%), SBPL (25%) and gold (15-17%), offset by LAP/HL growth (13-16%); floating-rate mortgages reprice up if the RBI hikes (FY28E). The cheque-clearance recognition change lifts yields marginally.
assumptions._feeIncomePctWhy: Non-interest operating income ÷ average AUM: 1.20% FY24, 1.27% FY25, 1.31% FY26 (incl. ₹439 cr assignment gains, lumpy). Insurance agency commission was ₹1,136 cr in FY26 (0.56% of AUM, ~16% of PBT). IRDAI's consultation paper of 23-Sep-2026 proposes capping commission on loan-linked insurance at ~2-5% (NBFC credit-life commissions now 7-47%). We assume a third of insurance commission is lost from FY28E (-0.15pp); the bear case loses most of it.
assumptions._costOfFundsWhy: Interest expense ÷ average Screener borrowings: 8.0% FY24, 8.1% FY25, 7.45% FY26; Q1FY27 annualised ~7.4%. CFO (28-Jul-2026): cost of funds flat for FY27 as a % of assets, up 5-10bp in H2, assuming a 25-50bp repo hike; a majority of economists expected a 25bp hike at the October policy (Moneycontrol poll, 28-Sep-2026). FY28E carries the full year of higher rates; ~25-30% of bank loans are MCLR-linked.
assumptions._opexPctWhy: Operating expenses incl. depreciation ÷ average business AUM: 3.3% FY24 (approx.), 3.25% FY26 (company basis 3.0-3.1% of assets). Guidance: opex ~3.0-3.1% of average assets with no operating leverage for 'another year or so' (360 new gold branches, 100 each in HL, LAP and CSEL). Q1 is seasonally the lowest-cost quarter (3.12% annualised). Gentle improvement from FY28E as gold branches mature (₹12-15 cr AUM each, break-even by next year-end).
assumptions._creditCostWhy: Provisions ÷ average business AUM: 1.05% FY24, 1.51% FY25, 1.73% FY26 (incl. a ₹200 cr overlay; 1.63% without). Company basis (on assets): 1.6% FY26 before the overlay, FY27 guidance ~1.5%, Q1FY27 1.5% (1.61% on our basis). Q1 is the seasonally worst quarter (Q1FY26 was 14-24bp above the FY26 full year), and management expects improvement from here. Against that, Stage 2+3 rose 49bp QoQ and vehicle-finance Stage 3 reached 4.05% (highest Q1 since Covid, Nomura). We take 1.50% (about 1.4-1.5% on the company's asset basis, in line with to slightly better than guidance; overlay kept, not released) and edge up to 1.55% in FY29E as CSEL, SBPL and gold (higher-loss products by design) grow faster.
assumptions._payoutWhy: Dividend has been ₹2.00 a share (100% of face value) every year since FY21; FY26 ₹2.00 = 3.3% of EPS. We assume ~3% (DPS ₹2.5-3.6).
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Screener 'other income' is mostly recoveries of written-off loans (₹415 cr of ₹466 cr in FY26; ₹254 cr in FY24-25) plus interest on tax refunds. TTM to Q1FY27 ₹484 cr; grows with the written-off pool.
assumptions._capitalRaiseWhy: Conversion of the last ₹630 cr of the ₹2,000 cr 7.5% CCDs (QIP, Oct-2023): 20,000 CCDs at ₹1,476.08 in Jul-2026 and 43,000 at ₹1,407.59 on 30-Sep-2026 (30.55 lakh shares). Debt becomes equity; no cash raised. Paid-up shares 85.751 cr after the 30-Sep allotment (NSE filing, 30-Sep-2026), incl. ~0.07 cr ESOP shares since March.

valuation._why: Ke = 6.5% + 1.15 × 6% = 13.4% (house rf and ERP; beta 1.15 for an AA+ rated, wholesale-funded vehicle and small-business lender, above Bajaj Finance's 1.1). sustainableRoe 19% = Chola's FY18-FY26 average (company basis 15-21%, median 20%) and what management's 3.5% pre-tax ROTA target gives at ~7x leverage. g = 10% long-run book growth (about nominal GDP). Residual income fades ROE to 19% over 8 years, payout rising to 25%, 6% terminal growth.

methods.name: P/B
methods.why: The street's method (Motilal Oswal 4.0x Mar-28E book, Emkay 3.8x FY28E, Prabhudas Lilladher 3.8x FY28E adjusted book). 3.2x = own median forward P/B since Apr-2021 (3.4x) × listed-lender P/B move vs five-year medians (−4.5%, eight peers excluding Chola) × growth regime 1.00 (our 20-22% AUM growth and ~20% ROE sit inside the window's range). Bull 3.7x = median since Apr-2023 (the FY24-FY26 years of 21-37% AUM growth); bear 2.7x = lowest since 2021.

methods.name: Justified P/B
methods.why: (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g) = (19 − 10) ÷ (13.4 − 10) on book at the 12-month target date.

methods.name: Residual income
methods.why: Book plus the present value of profit above the 13.4% cost of equity, ROE fading to 19%, rolled forward 6 months.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: Cross-check only. 17x = median forward P/E since Apr-2021 (19.4x, no trough years) × listed-lender P/E move vs five-year medians (−11.4%) × growth 1.00. Bull 20.6x = median since Apr-2023; bear 15x = lowest since 2021.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Growth re-accelerates (AUM +24/23/22%) as vehicle demand stays at record levels and mortgages scale; IRDAI caps do not bite (fees hold ~1.25% of AUM); credit cost falls to ~1.35% as CSEL and vehicle finance keep improving; long-run ROE 21%.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: Rate hikes and a weak monsoon: AUM +18/17/16%, funding 25bp dearer, most loan-linked insurance commission lost to IRDAI caps (−0.15pp), credit cost back to ~2.0% (FY21 Covid level on our basis) as vehicle-finance and LAP Stage 3 keep rising; long-run ROE 16%.
